rows.evidence: Q1: Results section <U+2013> the authors apply their own design methodology to example networks (Albacete sprinkler zone; 127.7 ha Valencia citrus drip network), running EPANET simulations and linear-programming runs to derive maximum/minimum demand curves (Fig. 5) and computing pumping-plant energy consumption for different pump configurations (Tables 8<U+2013>9, Fig. 6).
rows.notes: The study is a design-methodology paper with worked numerical examples (model runs, no field measurements). It does not report any result of its own on the investment cost of on-demand networks being higher, nor any comparison of on-demand versus rotation/restricted delivery. The statement that on-demand supply is expensive because large conveyance capacity is needed for peak demand appears only as a general assertion in the Introduction, not as a finding. Its own results concern: (i) hydrant discharge sizing with flow-limiting valves, which the authors say reduces investment by removing excess discharge; (ii) a method for maximum/minimum demand curves to dimension and regulate the pumping plant; (iii) simplified estimation of seasonal energy consumption under hourly electricity tariffs, including a 7,200 EUR investment difference for variable-speed drives with a 5.3-year payback. A remark that dimensioning for the most unfavourable hourly flow leads to further overdimensioning of pipes and pumps is a design observation, not a quantified own result on the claimed effect. Simulations are not compared with measurements from a real operating network.

notes: Full text appears complete (Introduction through References). Paper is methodological with illustrative application examples; no field validation of the design outputs.
